analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps from $4.25 to $5.75 an hour.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $5.75 an hour by 1997 never got a vote; it was referred to a Senate committee on January 11, 1995 and never acted on again.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $4.25 an hour to $4.75 in September 1995, $5.25 in 1996, and $5.75 in 1997. It also would have created a small commission to study automatically adjusting the minimum wage with inflation so it would not lose value between raises. The bill never left the Senate committee it was assigned to and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage — largely restaurant, retail, and service employees, many of them adults supporting families — would have seen their hourly pay rise by up to $1.50 over three years. The commission could have led to future raises keeping pace with inflation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers paid near the $4.25 minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $4.25 an hour to $4.75 on September 1, 1995, $5.25 on September 1, 1996, and $5.75 on September 1, 1997 — a 35% increase over three years for workers at the wage floor.

Creates a nine-member Commission on the Minimum Wage to recommend ways to restore the minimum wage to its historical level relative to average wages and to adjust it regularly, so it stops losing value between congressional raises.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that pay minimum-wage workers, especially restaurants, retail stores, and other small employers, would bear higher labor costs. Some of that cost would be passed to consumers through prices; some employers might reduce hours or entry-level hiring.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retailers, and other minimum-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Employers would face a 35% increase in the wage floor over three years. Small businesses and labor-intensive industries like restaurants argue that sharp increases raise costs, force price increases, and can reduce entry-level hiring — the standard objection to any large minimum wage hike.

The bill sets fixed dates rather than tying the wage to inflation, so the minimum would begin losing value again the moment the last step took effect; the commission only studies indexation and reports by September 1, 1997, without requiring Congress to act on its findings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A direct pay raise of up to $1.50 an hour for the lowest-paid workers is a large, concrete benefit, and most economic research finds modest employment effects at increases of this size. The real cost falls on small employers of low-wage labor, and some of it reaches consumers as higher prices. The bill's main design weakness is that it offers only one-time, fixed-step increases and merely studies — rather than adopts — inflation indexing. For context, Congress later enacted a smaller two-step increase to $5.15 an hour in 1996, below what this bill would have delivered.

outcome.mechanism: It was assigned to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, no action was ever taken on it there, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, joined by Senator Paul Wellstone as its only cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind is recorded for the rest of the 104th Congress, which ended January 3, 1997.
The Senate in this period had a 53-47 Republican majority, and the committee the bill sat in had a Republican chair; the bill never advanced past the referral step.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail, and other low-wage industries — were better off because the bill died, since they avoided the scheduled increases. Low-wage workers lost the most: Congress went on to pass a smaller increase, to $5.15 an hour in 1996, a dollar less than this bill's final step.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers; workers got less later

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Joined Kennedy in introducing the bill.

against.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Her committee took no recorded action on the bill after it was referred on January 11, 1995; no markup or hearing appears in the action history for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the bill's two sponsors were Democrats and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The most minimum-wage-intensive industry would have faced the largest cost increases from a 35% higher wage floor over three years. Its interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the pay raise workers would have received.
Retail, hospitality, and other employers of minimum-wage workers would have borne higher payroll costs and some pressure to raise prices or trim entry-level hiring.
